metadata.title: The Routing Key, Not the Token.
metadata.subtitle: The PagerDuty API Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude authenticate to PagerDuty the same way for every operation? Lands the carry-out that PagerDuty is really two separate APIs -- REST for reading and managing, Events v2 for triggering, acknowledging, and resolving -- each with its own auth scheme, and mixing them up produces a silent, empty-bodied failure rather than a clear error. The nbb cut takes the split apart and judges the design choice behind it.

beats.narration_text: Natural guess: one PagerDuty credential handles everything, so trigger an alert with your API token. It fails silently. Triggering doesn't take the token; it takes a routing key in the request body. Why the split?

beats.narration_text: Here's the split. PagerDuty runs two APIs on two different hosts, each authenticated its own way -- a design choice, not an accident. The REST API, at api dot pagerduty dot com, handles what you read and manage -- schedules, services, escalation policies, incidents, users. It authenticates with an Authorization header reading Token, then your key -- not Bearer, not Basic. Events v2, at events dot pagerduty dot com, handles the alert lifecycle instead -- triggering, acknowledging, resolving. It authenticates with a routing key sent in the request body, and sends no Authorization header at all. They optimized Events v2 for volume: any script or agent that can POST should fire an alert without carrying a long-lived token. REST is the opposite bet -- fewer callers, more sensitive operations, so it wants the token in the header. Under the hood, an alert fires on a service, routes through an escalation policy to specific schedules and users, opens an incident -- and every notification along the way is logged, which is the actual record of who got paged and why.

production_viz.label: TWO APIS, TWO AUTH SCHEMES
production_viz.caption: match the API to its auth scheme

beats.narration_text: Before you touch any data, run a sanity call -- GET slash v1 slash users slash me, with the Token header. A 200 means your credentials work. A 401 comes back with an empty body, and this is the trap: curl shows you nothing unless you explicitly ask for the status, with dash w or dash o slash dev slash null dash w. They optimized error responses for machines, not for people staring at a terminal -- honest about the failure, but only if you ask. Once you move from reading to writing, every mutation -- triggering, acknowledging, resolving -- needs a From header carrying a real email address. Leave it off and you get a 400 that looks like it came from nowhere.

A few more things worth knowing, because each one reveals another choice. Raw curl calls to the slash oncalls endpoint need dash g, or the bracket-style filters get mangled -- the bundled pd_oncall.sh script handles that for you. Any object you reference in a request body -- a service, an escalation policy -- needs both an id and a type field, or you get a 400 naming the missing one. Objects are strongly typed on purpose: more boilerplate, less ambiguity. Events v2 error responses come back as plain text, not JSON, so piping them through jq breaks immediately -- optimized for volume ingestion, not tidy client-side parsing. And the two APIs are rate-limited differently: REST gives you nine-sixty requests a minute with headers you can watch and back off from; Events v2 gives you no per-request header at all.

production_viz.label: NEEDS -g, ID+TYPE, RATE LIMITS DIFFER
production_viz.caption: REST 960/min with headers -- Events v2 has none

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. PagerDuty splits in two -- the REST API reads and manages everything with a Token header, while Events v2 triggers, acknowledges, and resolves alerts with a routing key in the body -- no token there at all. Mix them up, and you don't get an error message; you get an empty one.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read this with me, then paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to connect Claude to PagerDuty. For three tasks -- checking who's on call, triggering a test alert, and looking up why an incident paged someone -- tell me which API you'd call, which host, and exactly how you'd authenticate for each one, before you write any code. Go deeper: if you were designing a monitoring API from scratch, would you split reading and alerting the way PagerDuty did -- and what would you give up either way?
